title: Hosted API Overload SLOs and Error Budget Policy (Load Shedding Aware)
author: Aisha Bello
body:
## Purpose
This page updates how we define and alert on Hosted API SLOs now that **circuit breakers + load shedding** are being rolled out across the request path (gateway → routing/control plane → runtime).

We need two things simultaneously:
1) Preserve a strict definition of **platform reliability** (internal failures and regressions) and page on it quickly.
2) Avoid classifying **intentional, deterministic load shedding** (protective 429/503 with clear Redwood error codes + Retry-After) as “platform downtime,” while still tracking it as a capacity/experience signal.

This policy applies to **Hosted API** (multi-tenant) and is intended to be compatible with OpenAI-compatible endpoints and Redwood native endpoints.

---

## Definitions
### Request outcomes (SLO accounting categories)
Every request is classified into exactly one of the following outcomes for SLO and alerting.

| Outcome | Definition | Counted against Core Availability error budget? | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|
| success | Completed successfully (2xx) including streaming completed without server-side termination | No | Streaming success is defined as: stream opened AND terminal chunk delivered (or equivalent). |
| client_error | Customer-side request issue (4xx excluding overload-protected) | No | Examples: invalid params (400), auth (401/403), not found (404), request too large (413) when caused by customer input/policy. |
| overload_shed | Deterministic rejection or termination due to overload protection; returns documented status + Redwood overload code + Retry-After when retryable | No | This is the new category introduced by breakers/shedding. Tracked separately (see Overload Experience SLOs). |
| internal_error | Unexpected platform failure, bug, dependency outage, or ambiguous timeout; typically 5xx (excluding overload-mapped), gateway/routing/runtime errors, and internal timeouts | Yes | This is what our “Core Availability” SLO is meant to capture and page on. |

### “Overload-protected” errors
An error response is considered **overload-protected** only if all of the following are true:
- Status is **429** or **503** (see mapping notes below).
- Response includes a **Redwood overload error code** (header and/or JSON body depending on endpoint compatibility).
- For retryable cases, response includes **Retry-After** (seconds) with bounded values.
- Logs/traces include an overload reason that maps to one of the allowed overload codes.

If any of these conditions are missing (e.g., 503 with no Redwood code, 504 timeouts, connection resets), treat the error as **internal_error** for SLO purposes.

### Canonical Redwood overload error codes (SLO grouping)
The exact customer-facing schema is defined in ADR-0147; for SLO policy we group codes as follows:

**Admission / edge shedding**
- RW_OVERLOAD_ADMISSION
- RW_OVERLOAD_TIER_QUOTA_GUARD (only if explicitly documented as overload-protected; otherwise treat as client_error/quota)

**Breaker / routing shedding**
- RW_OVERLOAD_BREAKER_OPEN
- RW_OVERLOAD_CAPACITY_UNAVAILABLE

**Runtime / scheduler shedding**
- RW_OVERLOAD_QUEUE_FULL
- RW_OVERLOAD_PREFILL_SHED
- RW_OVERLOAD_DECODE_SHED
- RW_OVERLOAD_KV_CACHE_PRESSURE
- RW_OVERLOAD_MEMORY_PRESSURE

**Non-retryable overload-protected** (rare; still overload_shed but Retry-After may be omitted)
- RW_OVERLOAD_UNAVAILABLE_NO_RETRY

Notes:
- We intentionally keep the code list small in SLO alerting to avoid metric cardinality blowups; fine-grained analysis belongs in logs/traces.
- If a new overload code is added, Observability must update dashboards + this page before it is used for customer-facing behavior.

---

## SLO model (what we measure)
We split the SLOs into:
1) **Core Reliability SLOs**: should only degrade when we have internal failures.
2) **Overload Experience SLOs**: quantify how often we are forced to shed load and whether we do so “cleanly.”

This split is deliberate: shedding is an acceptable protective mechanism under extreme load, but it still impacts customers and should be visible with explicit targets and escalation paths.

### 1) Core Reliability SLOs (Hosted API)
#### SLO-HA1: Core Availability (excluding overload-protected errors)
**Goal:** 99.90% monthly

**SLI definition (request-based):**
- Numerator: requests that are **success** OR **client_error** OR **overload_shed**
- Denominator: all requests
- Failures: **internal_error** only

Rationale:
- This preserves a strict posture: a 500/timeout is always “our fault.”
- It prevents load shedding (which is intentionally returned with actionable guidance) from consuming availability error budget and masking true regressions.

**Important:** If we return 503/429 without proper overload metadata, it is not overload-protected and will count as **internal_error**.

#### SLO-HA2: Successful completion for admitted requests (quality of service once accepted)
**Goal:** 99.95% monthly

**SLI definition:**
- Denominator: requests that were **admitted** past the gateway admission point (i.e., not edge-shed)
- Failure: internal_error for admitted requests (including runtime failures, routing failures, mid-stream server terminations)

Rationale:
- Admission control can keep core availability “green” while admitted requests still fail due to runtime regressions. This SLO catches that.

#### SLO-HA3: Tail latency (admitted requests)
We use latency SLOs as guardrails; they do not consume “availability” error budget but can page via burn-style alerting when severe.

Targets (per region, per model class; defaults below):
- **p95** end-to-end latency (non-streaming): ≤ 2.5s
- **p99** end-to-end latency (non-streaming): ≤ 8.0s
- **time-to-first-token (TTFT)** (streaming): p95 ≤ 1.5s, p99 ≤ 5.0s

Measurement scope:
- Only for **admitted requests** (exclude overload_shed).
- Segment by: region, model, route, customer tier (at minimum prod vs dev/free), streaming vs non-streaming.

---

### 2) Overload Experience SLOs (Hosted API)
These SLOs make overload visible without conflating it with downtime.

#### SLO-OE1: Overload-protected error hygiene (correct semantics)
**Goal:** ≥ 99.5% of overload-triggered responses are “well-formed”

Definition:
- Among responses where any layer triggered overload protection, the response must include:
  - documented 429/503 mapping,
  - Redwood overload code,
  - Retry-After when retryable,
  - OpenAI-compat error object mapping where applicable.

Failure examples:
- Gateway returns plain 503 without Redwood code.
- Runtime sheds and the gateway times out, resulting in 504.

#### SLO-OE2: Overload shedding rate (capacity pressure signal)
**Goal (default):** ≤ 0.50% monthly of total requests are overload_shed for Production tiers.

Notes:
- This is a starting target for 2026H1; it is expected to be revisited once canary data is stable.
- This SLO is segmented and reviewed by region/model. A global aggregate can hide concentrated hotspots.

#### SLO-OE3: Breaker stability (avoid flapping)
**Goal:** ≤ 2 breaker state transitions per (region, model, tier) per 10 minutes (steady state)

Notes:
- This is a stability guardrail to prevent oscillation that can amplify customer retries.

---

## Error budget accounting policy
### What consumes the Core Availability error budget
Only **internal_error** consumes the Core Availability (SLO-HA1) error budget.

Internal errors include:
- 5xx other than overload-mapped 429/503
- 504/gateway timeouts
- connection resets attributable to our edge/runtime
- ambiguous “upstream error” without overload metadata
- routing failures (e.g., no healthy backends) unless explicitly mapped as overload-protected capacity unavailable with correct semantics

### What does NOT consume the Core Availability error budget
- overload_shed (properly formed overload-protected errors)
- client_error (auth/validation issues, customer misuse)

### When overload still triggers escalation
Overload doesn’t consume Core Availability budget, but it *does* trigger escalation when it violates Overload Experience SLOs or operational thresholds:
- sustained overload_shed rate
- breaker opens sustained for production tiers
- missing Retry-After / malformed overload payloads
- sudden shift from overload_shed to internal_error (indicates broken overload plumbing)

### “Gray failure” rule
If we cannot confidently classify an error as overload_shed (missing code/headers, inconsistent mapping, sampling gaps), it is treated as **internal_error** by default.

This biases SLO accounting toward surfacing problems in the overload protection implementation.

---

## Alerting policy (paging vs ticketing)
### Pager-worthy (Sev2+ signals)
These alerts should page the Hosted API oncall/SRE rotation.

1) **Core Availability burn (SLO-HA1)**
- Page on fast burn (example): 2% error budget consumed in 1 hour OR 5% in 6 hours (final thresholds maintained in SLO toolkit)
- Condition: internal_error rate elevated across a meaningful traffic volume

2) **Admitted request failure burn (SLO-HA2)**
- Page when admitted internal_error rate exceeds threshold even if overload_shed is high/low

3) **Overload hygiene regression (SLO-OE1)**
- Page if malformed overload responses exceed 0.5% of overload-triggered responses for 15 minutes
- Rationale: malformed responses create retry storms and ambiguous customer incidents

4) **Overload turns into internal failures**
- Page when we observe simultaneous:
  - increasing overload signals (breaker open / queue saturation)
  - AND a rising share of timeouts/5xx without overload metadata

### Non-paging (ticket/Slack + business-hours response)
1) **Moderate overload_shed rate without internal errors**
- Create ticket and notify #eng-sre + #eng-platform with region/model breakdown.
- Escalate to page only if it breaches agreed sustained thresholds (below).

2) **Breaker flapping at low impact**
- File ticket to tune hysteresis/cooldowns (owners: SRE + Smart Routing).

### Sustained overload escalation thresholds (default)
These are operational triggers, not “downtime.” They are meant to catch customer-impacting capacity issues.

For Production tiers:
- Page if overload_shed > 5% for 15 minutes in a region for a top-5 model OR
- Page if breaker remains open > 10 minutes for a top-5 model in a region and admitted success rate degrades OR
- Page if Retry-After median value rises above 30s for 10 minutes (indicates prolonged recovery)

For Dev/Free tiers:
- Notify via Slack; page only if correlated with internal_error burn.

---

## Implementation notes (metrics, queries, and segmentation)
Canonical metrics are specified in the observability standard page. For SLO computations, we require at minimum:
- `redwood_requests_total{service="gateway", outcome=..., route=..., model=..., region=..., tier=..., streaming=...}`
- `redwood_overload_responses_total{code=..., layer=..., region=..., model=..., tier=...}`
- `redwood_breaker_state{state=..., region=..., model=..., tier=...}`
- `redwood_request_latency_seconds_bucket{admitted="true", ...}`
- `redwood_ttft_seconds_bucket{admitted="true", streaming="true", ...}`

Cardinality constraints:
- `route` must be a bounded set (documented API routes). Do not label by customer_id.
- `model` is the served model name (bounded by catalog).
- `tier` is an enum (free/dev/prod/enterprise, etc.).

### PromQL-style examples (illustrative)
**Core availability error rate (internal failures only):**
- sum(rate(redwood_requests_total{outcome="internal_error"}[5m])) / sum(rate(redwood_requests_total[5m]))

**Overload shed rate:**
- sum(rate(redwood_requests_total{outcome="overload_shed"}[5m])) / sum(rate(redwood_requests_total[5m]))

**Malformed overload rate (hygiene):**
- sum(rate(redwood_overload_responses_total{well_formed="false"}[5m])) / sum(rate(redwood_overload_responses_total[5m]))

These are examples only; the source of truth for alert thresholds and windows is the SLO toolkit configuration.

---

## Operational guidance
### During an incident
- If Core Availability is burning: treat as a normal reliability incident (dependency outage, deploy regression, infra issue).
- If overload_shed is high but Core Availability is not burning: treat as a capacity/traffic-management incident.
  - Primary owners: SRE + Smart Routing + Runtime (depending on layer signals).
  - Use the Hosted Overload Mitigation Runbook.

### After rollout changes
Any change that affects outcome classification or overload mapping must include:
- validation that overload_shed is properly tagged,
- a canary review of the SLO dashboards,
- confirmation that ambiguous 5xx/504 do not increase.

---

## Reporting and review cadence
- Weekly: SRE review of SLO-HA1/HA2 burn events and top internal_error causes.
- Weekly (until full rollout stable): Overload Experience review (SLO-OE1/OE2/OE3) with Smart Routing + Runtime.
- Monthly: Reliability Program report-out: incident counts, p99 latency trends, overload_shed trends, and top mitigation actions.

---

## Change log
- 2025-10-22: Initial policy drafted (Aisha Bello) to support Hosted overload protection program.
- 2025-12-09: Added Overload Experience SLOs and hygiene requirements; clarified “gray failure” rule.
- 2026-01-22: Updated escalation thresholds and clarified admitted-request SLO (HA2) after us-east canary learnings.
